# The AI Value Chain {#sec-market-structure}

A model call looks like a software service, but it is the visible end of an
industrial chain. Depending on the deployment, an accepted outcome may require
chip fabrication, memory and packaging, deliverable power, accelerator capacity,
a model artifact or hosted service, a gateway, an application, data rights, and
a working organizational process. Those links form a dependency graph, not one
market. A local model can bypass a hosted API, for example, while still depending
on hardware, power, software, and licensed data.

@sec-economics compared the cost of feasible alternatives from one buyer's
perspective. This chapter asks what shapes the terms offered to that buyer. The
answer is specific to a workload: which dependency is scarce or difficult to
replace, who controls it, and which outside options, the alternatives the buyer
could turn to instead, can deliver the same accepted outcome. Bargaining power
grows when credible alternatives disappear, not because a company appears at
several layers.

## Map dependencies before naming a market

A value-chain diagram describes technical and contractual dependence. It does
not establish that every box is a market, that every edge is a purchase, or that
one company owns the whole path.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-market-structure-chain
//| fig-cap: "Technical dependencies in a deployed AI capability. Boxes are not market boundaries, and some deployments bypass a box: the dashed edge is an application that calls a local model directly, without a gateway."
digraph ai_value_chain {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.12;
  ranksep=0.22;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1",
        margin="0.10,0.07"];
  edge [color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.6];
  I [label="Critical inputs\nhardware | power | data rights"];
  C [label="Compute capacity\naccelerators | regions | networks"];
  M [label="Model capability\nartifact | hosted service"];
  A [label="Access layer\ngateway | policy | routing"];
  W [label="Workflow\napplication | people | distribution"];
  O [label="Accepted outcome\nquality | service | policy"];
  // One group keeps the dependency chain in a straight column; the bypass
  // edge runs beside it.
  I [group=main]; C [group=main]; M [group=main];
  A [group=main]; W [group=main]; O [group=main];
  I -> C -> M -> A -> W -> O;
  M -> W [label="local model,\nno gateway", style=dashed, fontsize=9,
          constraint=false];
}
```

The OECD's 2025 review describes AI compute infrastructure as a multilayer supply
chain with concentrated segments, high entry barriers, vertical relationships,
partnerships, switching barriers, and occasional shortages. It also warns that
its reported supplier shares are bottleneck indicators, not the result of one
global market-definition exercise [@oecd2025competition]. The UK Competition
and Markets Authority (CMA) similarly identifies compute, data, technical
expertise, funding, and routes to market as possible constraints on entry or
expansion in foundation-model services [@cma2024foundation]. These are risks and
dependencies to investigate, not proof that one company has power everywhere.

A **bottleneck** is a dependency whose available capacity or terms constrain the
workload. A **control point** is narrower: a supplier controls a scarce or
hard-to-replace input, has the ability and incentive to change access or terms,
and the buyer has too few effective outside options to respond. A long lead time
can reveal a bottleneck. It does not by itself prove market power, a supplier's
ability to raise prices or worsen terms without losing enough customers to make
the change unprofitable. Technical superiority, company size, or a high market
share calculated over an undefined denominator does not prove it either.

| Layer under review | Candidate unit | Possible constraint | Evidence to retain |
|---|---|---|---|
| Advanced compute | deliverable accelerator-hours in the required region and period | hardware, power, networking, or allocation | accepted orders, queue time, outages, utilization, rejected demand |
| Model service | accepted results at the required quality and service level | capability, quota, policy, or support | matched evaluations, quotas, incidents, price and model history |
| Application channel | completed workflows for the target customer group | distribution, procurement, identity, or integration | acquisition path, approval time, active users, viable competing workflows |
| Data rights | usable records under the required purpose and jurisdiction | license, consent, provenance, or deletion obligations | contracts, lineage, permitted uses, unresolved claims |

The same supplier can appear in several rows, and two rows can be complements
(inputs needed together) rather than substitutes (inputs that can replace each
other). A share therefore needs a declared market boundary before it is
computed.

## Define the market before calculating shares

Concentration, the degree to which a few suppliers account for most of a
market's sales, has a long measurement history. Albert Hirschman in 1945 and
Orris Herfindahl in 1950 independently developed closely related share-squared
indexes; Rhoades later summarized their origin and regulatory use
[@rhoades1993hhi]. The arithmetic is simple once the denominator is fixed; most
of the analysis goes into deciding which sales and suppliers belong in it.

Record a candidate market as

$$
\mathcal{M} = (P, G, T, U, Q).
$$

Here, $P$ means the product or service being tested, $G$ its geography, $T$ the
time window, $U$ the customer group, and $Q$ the minimum quality and service
threshold. The tuple is an analytical record, not a claim that only one market
definition is valid. A candidate belongs in $\mathcal{M}$ only if customers in
$U$ would treat it as a reasonable substitute for $P$ under the declared
geography, period, and threshold.

For example, a downloadable model and a managed frontier API are both ways to
obtain model output. They are not necessarily substitutes for a hospital that
requires a particular accuracy, region, audit trail, support contract, and
response-time objective. Conversely, two APIs with different model names may be
close substitutes if both pass the same evaluation and service contract. Define
the decision first and derive the candidate set from it, rather than from a
vendor's product category.

A share also needs a unit. Revenue can reflect what customers pay. Delivered
capacity can better describe a homogeneous input whose competitive significance
comes from the ability to expand. Usage can describe an operating service, while
new-customer wins can reveal current competition better than a large installed
base. The 2023 U.S. Merger Guidelines explicitly permit different share metrics
when they better match market reality [@doj2023merger]. For an AI service, report
at least two defensible proxies when the data allow, such as revenue and accepted
workload volume, and explain omissions.

Given a defined market, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) is

$$
\operatorname{HHI}(\mathcal{M})
= 10{,}000 \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i^2,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i = 1.
$$

Here, $n$ is the number of suppliers in $\mathcal{M}$ and $s_i$ is the share of
supplier $i$, expressed from zero to one; all supplier shares sum to one. The
factor $10{,}000$ puts the result on the conventional zero-to-10,000 scale.
Squaring gives larger suppliers more weight. The equal-sized equivalent count
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}=10{,}000/\operatorname{HHI}$ denotes the number of equal-sized
suppliers that would produce the same index, a limited but intuitive reading.

The HHI is a screening statistic, not a finding of market power. Under the 2023
U.S. Merger Guidelines, a post-merger HHI above 1,800 combined with an increase
above 100 points creates a structural presumption in that merger framework, a
rebuttable presumption that the merger may substantially lessen competition
[@doj2023merger]. Those thresholds are not a universal grading scale for
technology markets. A result changes when the market boundary, share metric,
missing suppliers, or time window changes.

Three hypothetical share vectors, not estimates of any AI market, show that
sensitivity. Four suppliers holding 45, 30, 15, and 10 percent give an HHI of
3,250, about 3.1 effective firms. Five suppliers at 30, 25, 20, 15, and 10
percent give 2,250 and 4.4 effective firms, and five equal suppliers give 2,000
and exactly five.

A supplier count alone would call all three cases similar. The HHI distinguishes
their size distributions, but it still cannot tell whether entry is timely,
capacity is available, customers can switch, or providers compete on dimensions
that the selected share misses.

```{figure}
//| figure: market-concentration
//| label: fig-market-structure-hhi
//| fig-cap: "The HHI as area, for the chapter's hypothetical share lists, not estimates of any AI market. Each supplier's share is the side of a square on the diagonal of the unit square, so the square's area is $s_i^2$ and the covered fraction of the unit square is HHI / 10,000. A merger replaces the two suppliers' squares with one of side $s_a + s_b$ (outlined); the hatched rectangles are the area it adds, $\Delta\mathrm{HHI} = 2 \cdot 10{,}000\, s_a s_b$, and the readout tests the result against the 2023 guidelines' thresholds (post-merger HHI above 1,800 and an increase above 100). Widening the boundary gives the chosen share of sales to four equal outside sellers (gray) and scales the named shares down by the same factor."
market: narrow
merge: CD
widen: 0
```

## Separate scale economies, concentration, and power

Large fixed cost can lower average cost without lowering marginal cost. In the
simple cost function

$$
C(q)=F+cq,
\qquad
AC(q)=\frac{F}{q}+c,
\qquad
MC(q)=c,
$$

$q$ denotes output, $C(q)$ total cost, $F$ fixed cost, and $c$ constant cost for
one additional unit. $AC(q)$ is average cost and $MC(q)$ is marginal cost. As
output rises, the fixed term $F/q$ falls, which is the simplest form of
economies of scale, while marginal cost remains $c$. A shortcut that combines
high fixed cost, falling marginal cost, and switching cost (what a customer
spends to move to another supplier) into one condition therefore mixes three
distinct mechanisms.

High concentration can arise from innovation, capacity constraints, economies of
scale, regulation, or exclusionary conduct, meaning conduct that raises rivals'
costs or blocks their access to inputs or customers. It can coexist with
aggressive competition for the next contract, or with weak competition inside an
installed base. Evidence of power comes from behavior and alternatives:
persistent price or term changes that customers cannot avoid, denied or delayed
access to an input, poor expansion by rivals despite demand, contractual
restrictions, or failed switching attempts.

The scope of a measurement determines what its shares describe. In its July 2025
UK cloud investigation, the CMA estimated 2024 infrastructure-as-a-service
revenue shares of 40-50 percent for AWS, 30-40 percent for Microsoft, and 5-10
percent for Google. Platform-as-a-service shares were less concentrated. The
same appendix says accelerated-compute revenue could not be separated
consistently and was a small part of the measured total [@cma2025cloud]. This is
evidence about specified UK cloud services, not a direct estimate of a global
AI-compute or model market.

### Do not infer profit from a price chart

Listed price is not production cost. Revenue is not gross profit, gross profit
is not economic rent (the return beyond what would keep the capital in its
current use), and capital expenditure is not a layer's share of customer value.
A valid margin comparison needs an audited segment or a reproducible allocation
rule for shared hardware, labor, research, energy, and overhead. A return above
the cost of capital can motivate further analysis, but it still does not
identify which mechanism caused the return.

The same boundary applies to a profit-pool table, which divides an industry's
profit among its layers. A table built from one investor's unaudited estimate
across heterogeneous companies and layers cannot show how one token's payment is
divided, and a two-point trend cannot support a decade-long forecast. Where
segment reporting is unavailable, say that profit allocation is unknown and
measure the contract terms visible to the buyer.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

Korinek and Vipra argue that several mechanisms may make frontier-model markets
more concentrated over time: economies of scale and scope (the second meaning
savings from producing several products with shared inputs), feedback, user
inertia, and vertical integration, one company operating at successive layers of
the chain. Their published analysis also describes strong current competition
and treats future tipping, a market's shift toward one dominant supplier, as
conditional, not as an observed natural monopoly [@korinek2025concentrating].

Natural monopoly has a stricter cost meaning. For total demand $Q$, one supplier's
cost must be no greater than the combined cost of every feasible split:

$$
C(Q) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{m} C(q_j),
\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{m} q_j = Q.
$$

Here, $m$ is the number of producing firms in a proposed split and $q_j$ is firm
$j$'s output. The inequality expresses cost subadditivity over the relevant
demand, a central condition in natural-monopoly analysis [@sharkey1978supportable].
High training cost, a high HHI, or customer switching cost does not establish
that condition. Treat the frontier-concentration thesis as a scenario to test
against the evidence for each model service.
:::

## Measure switching as a directed path

A buyer's outside option is credible only if it can be exercised. API syntax
compatibility covers one of several layers a migration must cross. Record at
least five layers:

1. **Interface portability:** request, response, tool, identity, and error
   schemas can be translated.
2. **State and data portability:** prompts, retrieval indexes, tool definitions,
   fine-tuning data, evaluation sets, logs, and user state can be exported under
   usable rights.
3. **Behavioral portability:** the replacement passes the same quality, policy,
   and service evaluation.
4. **Artifact and runtime portability:** weights, tokenizer, configuration, and
   inference code can run on another supported stack.
5. **Operational and commercial portability:** regions, quota, observability,
   support, price, and contract terms remain feasible.

Switching cost is directional. Moving from supplier $a$ to supplier $b$ can cost
more than moving back because formats, rights, team knowledge, and capacity
differ. A useful ledger is

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{\mathrm{switch}}(a \rightarrow b)
&= C_{\mathrm{export}} + C_{\mathrm{rewrite}} + C_{\mathrm{retest}} \\
&\quad + C_{\mathrm{parallel}} + C_{\mathrm{exit}}
+ \mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{failure}}].
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $C_{\mathrm{export}}$ covers state transfer and data egress;
$C_{\mathrm{rewrite}}$ covers interface and workflow changes;
$C_{\mathrm{retest}}$ covers evaluation, security, and compliance work;
$C_{\mathrm{parallel}}$ covers running both paths during migration; and
$C_{\mathrm{exit}}$ covers termination and stranded commitments.
$\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{failure}}]$ is expected loss from migration failures.
The arrow records direction.

Estimate those terms with a migration drill. Export representative state, route a
held-out workload to the replacement, measure quality and tail latency, remove
the old path, record time to restore service, and test rollback. Only a fallback
that has passed this exercise counts as an outside option.

## Read vertical integration through rights and incentives

Vertical integration can lower coordination cost, secure investment, improve
hardware-software co-design, and make capacity planning more reliable. It can
also create preferential access, raise rivals' input costs, restrict
multihoming (a customer's use of several suppliers at once), or enable
foreclosure, cutting rivals off from a route to market. The label alone does
not determine the effect, and it does not make every integration
anticompetitive.

The Federal Trade Commission's January 2025 staff report examined specific
relationships among the cloud providers Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft and the
developers Anthropic and OpenAI. It documented varying equity and revenue rights,
consultation or control provisions, cloud-spend commitments, discounted compute,
exclusivity terms, product integration, and access to sensitive technical and
business information [@ftc2025partnerships]. Staff identified possible effects
on input access and switching. The report did not define every AI market or make
an illegality finding, and its evidence should not be generalized beyond the
studied arrangements.

For procurement, map the rights that change behavior:

- committed spend and the share of expected demand it covers;
- capacity priority, reservation, and shortage allocation;
- exclusivity, preferred-provider, and multicloud terms;
- ownership and permitted use of prompts, outputs, telemetry, and derived data;
- model, product, and intellectual-property licenses;
- governance, information, audit, price-change, termination, and exit rights.

Usage does not automatically become training data or a competitive flywheel, a
loop in which more usage improves the product and the improved product attracts
more usage. Separate product telemetry, evaluation data, training data,
distribution feedback, and revenue. For each loop, record what information
moves, under which right, how quickly it changes the product, and whether a
rival can obtain an equivalent input.

## Distinguish openness, transparency, and contestability

Open Source AI requires more than available weights. The Open Source
Initiative's 2024 definition asks for freedoms to use, study, modify, and share
the system, together with data information, code, and parameters in the preferred
form for modification [@opensource2024osaid]. It is a community standard rather
than a universal legal definition, but it makes the missing materials explicit.

Broadly available weights can enable inspection, adaptation, and self-hosting.
They can improve a buyer's outside options when the license permits the use, the
artifact is complete, a supported runtime exists, the candidate passes the
evaluation contract, and sufficient capacity is obtainable. If any one of those
conditions fails, weight access does not create a production substitute. Kapoor
and colleagues present competition benefits of open-weight releases as plausible
but qualified, alongside distinct benefits and risks [@kapoor2024societal].

A license can also restrict who may run the weights for others. Some open-weight
licenses require a separate agreement from companies that sell hosted access above
a revenue threshold, so a buyer's own deployment may be permitted while a
third-party host serving the same weights needs the developer's consent;
@sec-model-landscape records examples. For a buyer that runs the model internally,
or stays below the threshold, self-hosting remains an outside option; a buyer that
wants a third-party host for those weights depends on that host's agreement with
the developer.

Capability sets a further condition. An open-weight release is a substitute only
for workloads it can pass, so its distance from the closed frontier matters.
Independent evaluators usually express that distance as a lag: the time between a
closed model first reaching a capability level and the best open-weight model
reaching it. A buyer whose workload is met at that earlier level has an open-weight
candidate to evaluate; a buyer who needs the current frontier does not. The
measured lag depends on the benchmark set (public or held out, and which domains),
the aggregation method, whether closed models were run with their safeguards
disabled, and which releases are compared, so each estimate is read with those
conditions attached.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Epoch AI estimates that since January 2026 the most capable open-weight models have
trailed frontier closed models by an average of four months on its Epoch
Capabilities Index, an aggregate of many benchmark results, with an average gap of
8 index points [@epoch2026openclosed]. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation
(CAISI) placed DeepSeek V4 Pro, evaluated in April 2026 on nine benchmarks that
include held-out sets, about eight months behind the US frontier and close to
GPT-5 [@caisi2026deepseekv4]. Its September assessment of GLM-5.3 put that model
about four months behind on an aggregate of cyber benchmarks, without comparing
models not yet released [@caisi2026glm53]. In a joint UK AISI and CAISI cyber-range
test, Kimi K3 reached step 17 of a 32-step attack path on average, against 28.5 for
the most cyber-capable US models, which ran with system-level safeguards disabled
[@aisi2026kimik3]. Artificial Analysis reported in April 2026 a 6-point gap on its
Intelligence Index between the best open-weight models and GPT-5.5, widest on hard
reasoning, physics, and terminal-coding tasks, with three recent open-weight models
offering comparable scores at one-half to one-sixth of the price of leading closed
models [@artificialanalysis2026openweights]. The estimates differ in model, date,
benchmark set, and method.
:::

Transparency is another axis. The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index
reported a mean score of 40.69 out of 100, about 41, compared with 58 in 2024;
training data, training compute, and post-deployment usage and impact were among
the weakest areas [@wan2025fmti]. The indicator set changed substantially in
2025, the sampled companies changed, and only nine companies appeared in both
editions. The headline decline is therefore not a clean like-for-like time
series. The index measures public disclosure, not model quality, safety, market
concentration, or switching cost.

Transparency can improve comparison, risk assessment, and accountability. It does
not by itself create a substitute. A layer is contestable when challengers can
obtain critical inputs, enter and expand, and reach customers, and when
customers can switch or multihome without prohibitive technical or contractual
friction.

## Match each claim to evidence

| Claim | Evidence that can support it | What the evidence does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| The market is concentrated | declared $\mathcal{M}$, complete shares, defensible denominator, sensitivity to boundary and metric | market power, harm, or cause |
| An input is a control point | shortages, allocation rules, lead times, substitutes, expansion attempts, ability and incentive | that every downstream buyer is constrained |
| Customers are locked in | completed migration drill, directional cost, failed exits, commitment and termination terms | that a compatible API or available weights remove lock-in |
| Integration changes competition | contract rights, information flows, preferential treatment, rival access, observed conduct | that ownership or partnership alone is harmful |
| A layer earns persistent excess return | audited segment profit, capital employed, opportunity cost, stable allocation rule | how one token's payment is divided or why the return exists |
| A layer is contestable | timely entry and expansion, input access, customer reach, switching and multihoming evidence | that a large model catalog equals effective choice |

Evidence should have a date. Supplier shares, model quality, licensing terms,
capacity, and partnerships change at different speeds. Preserve the quote,
contract, measurement method, and market boundary used for each conclusion.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

@sec-powering-ai supplies the physical capacity and time-to-power evidence;
@sec-data-rights-economics supplies the rights and provenance boundary; and
@sec-economics supplies the accepted-result ledger. Market structure adds the
availability and credibility of alternatives. A lower model price matters only
if the alternative can obtain the required inputs and pass the same workload,
service, policy, and exit tests.
:::

## Operate a market record

Run the analysis as a dated, repeatable review:

1. **Define the decision.** State the outcome being procured and why a market
   question affects it.
2. **Freeze the market boundary.** Record product or service, geography, time
   window, customer group, and quality and service threshold.
3. **Enumerate suppliers.** Include current suppliers, committed entrants,
   self-supply where relevant, and the reason each candidate is or is not a
   reasonable substitute.
4. **Measure more than one share proxy.** Reconcile revenue, capacity, usage,
   accepted workload, or new-customer measures and disclose missing data.
5. **Test matched alternatives.** Run the same evaluation and service contract
   against candidates rather than counting names or endpoints.
6. **Map dependencies and rights.** Record input suppliers, ownership, spend
   commitments, information flows, capacity rights, price changes, and
   termination terms.
7. **Exercise migration.** Perform the directed switch, measure cash and time to
   restore service, and verify rollback.
8. **Set review triggers.** Reopen the analysis after a material price, model,
   license, capacity, partnership, regulation, or workload change.
9. **Refresh the record.** Replace forecasts with observed shares, incidents,
   migrations, and contract outcomes; retain the old record for comparison.

The record should contain the workload and acceptance-rule digest, candidate
list, exclusion reasons, share data and denominator, HHI sensitivity, contract
versions, dependency owners, migration evidence, unresolved assumptions, and
review date. That package lets another team reproduce the conclusion instead of
inheriting a label such as "concentrated" or "open."

@sec-adoption-productivity moves from supplier choice to realized work. A market
can offer several credible alternatives while none creates user value, or one
supplier can hold a strong position while a narrow workflow still produces
positive returns. The next chapter measures when a deployed capability produces
that value inside an organization.
